flags.finding: [partially supported] In S001, the screenplay depicts a comedic stunt sequence where Jordan physically grabs a performer with dwarfism in costume and throws him across the bullpen toward a giant velcro dartboard, sending the performer hurtling through the air. Staging this sequence requires wire-rigging / body harness flying rigs, spotters, deceleration capture equipment, and strict performer safety protocols overseen by a licensed Stunt Coordinator. Under CSATF Safety Bulletin #4 (Stunts), all flying rigging must be tested and inspected prior to execution, and an on-site safety meeting and walk-through dry-run must precede the stunt. Additionally, production must conduct a dignity and safety consultation with the cast member to ensure safe, ethical, and consensual execution of the gag, utilizing specialized stunt rigging and potential VFX takeover for the impact.

citations.excerpt: All equipment used for rigging must be inspected to check for wear, damage, and integrity prior to use. The Stunt Coordinator should approve the use of all rigging equipment. Any equipment found to be defective shall be removed from service. Fall protection may be required when rigging at heights.

remedy.detail: Engage a dedicated SAG-AFTRA Stunt Coordinator and specialized stunt rigger to design and execute a wire-flying harness setup with deceleration capture pads or digital green-screen composite/VFX takeover for the target impact. Employ a trained stunt double for the aerial flight and conduct a pre-shoot performer dignity and safety review. Costs vary by shooting region and union agreements.

flags.finding: [partially supported] Scene S002 depicts high-speed precision sports car driving on the Long Island Expressway (L.I.E.), with a Ferrari Testarossa zooming and weaving aggressively in and out of active traffic while the driver is distracted. Staging high-speed vehicle maneuvers and traffic weaving cannot be performed on open public roadways without controlled conditions. Under CSATF Safety Bulletin #43 (Recommended Guidelines for Free Driving) and vehicle stunt protocols, shooting moving vehicle sequences with complex driver actions requires Intermittent Traffic Control (ITC) or full road closures, location filming permits, police escorts, and the hiring of professional precision/stunt drivers or a process trailer / low-boy rig.

flags.finding: [partially supported] Scenes S006 and S089 depict nighttime helicopter flight, low-altitude hovering at 30 feet over a residential estate (pool, tennis court), and a hard, uncontrolled descent/crash-landing onto a grass driving range, followed by the pilot/passenger exiting near the spinning aircraft. Low-altitude night aerial operations and simulated hard landings pose severe aviation hazards. remedy.detail: Engage a SAG-AFTRA Stunt Coordinator and professional stunt double fitted with concealed high-density foam padding and impact armor. Install temporary foam padding or disguised step-edge cushioning on the concrete stairs and place crash mats at the asphalt base just out of frame. Conduct rehearsals and night lighting checks before recording. Costs vary by shooting region and union agreements.

flags.finding: [partially supported] In S151, a character chokes and falls backward, crashing into and entirely shattering a large glass kitchen table, followed by aggressive physical resuscitation (CPR chest compressions, simulated broken ribs, vomiting). Crashing through practical plate glass presents severe laceration and puncture hazards. Under CSATF Safety Bulletin #4 (Stunts), standard safety protocols mandate replacing all plate glass with custom breakaway tempered sugar glass, resin, or SMASH plastic. The fall must be staged by a stunt double or trained actor wearing hidden back/elbow impact padding, with debris clearance and eye protection protocols in place.

citations.excerpt: The Stunt Coordinator will review the PPE with Production Management and/or the designated representative to ensure studio requirements are followed. remedy.detail: Engage a Stunt Coordinator and special effects prop maker to fabricate a custom breakaway resin/sugar glass table with pre-scored rounded break points. Equip the performer/stunt double with back, hip, and elbow impact armor, place concealed landing pads under set rugs if needed, and conduct safety sweeps for sharp fragments between takes. Costs vary by shooting region and union agreements.

flags.finding: [partially supported] Across multiple scenes, live animals are featured on set: a live chimpanzee, reptiles (snakes, iguanas, turtles) in a crowded trading bullpen (S049), a Maltese dog (S062, S179), and Donnie grabbing a live goldfish from a bowl and swallowing it whole (S098). Under CSATF Safety Bulletin #6 (Animal Handling Rules for the Motion Picture Industry) and American Humane Association "No Animals Were Harmed" standards, live animals must be supervised by qualified professional trainers/wranglers, USDA-licensed handlers for exotic primates and reptiles, and have veterinary care available. Crucially, harming or ingesting live animals (such as a live goldfish) is strictly prohibited on film sets; the swallowing gag must be executed using a food-grade simulated gelatin prop fish or VFX composite.

The exposure here represents potential defense costs rather than liability for damages.

citations.title: Using Trademarks in Film and TV
citations.excerpt: However, even if you have the right to use a trademark, you do not have the right to commit trade libel in the name of entertainment. Trade libel occurs when a product or service is falsely accused of some bad attribute. For example, if you showed someone eating a McDonald’s hamburger or drinking a Coca-Cola and he or she immediately keeled over dead because the food or drink was poisonous, that would libel the trademark. Corporations live and die by their trademarks. A filmmaker has every right to dress sets with real products, but no right to disparage a trademark. If the movie does not misrepresent the source of the product there is typically no prohibition of the use of a trademark in a film.

remedy.detail: If production counsel or E&O insurer requests risk mitigation, replace 'McDonald’s' in dialogue with a generic fast food reference (e.g., 'flipping burgers' or 'at a fast-food joint') during production or via ADR at zero to negligible cost. Alternatively, production counsel may elect to retain the line as written as protected character dialogue under First Amendment principles, backed by a standard docudrama disclaimer.
